extracted.intended_audience: comic publishers, creators, historians, and researchers interested in content regulation and censorship in comics
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or producing U.S. comic-book content to meet the Comics Code Authority (CCA) standards and obtain the CCA seal; includes the original 1954 Code provisions and later revisions (1971 etc.) that modified allowances for violence, drugs, and supernatural elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crimes must not create sympathy for criminals
rubrics_metrics.description: Crimes shall never be presented in such a way as to create sympathy for the criminal, to promote distrust of the forces of law and justice, or to inspire others with a desire to imitate criminals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a core moral requirement: depictions of crime must not glamorize criminals or undermine faith in law enforcement; later revisions allowed limited sympathetic depiction only if exceptional and punished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of excessive violence
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes of excessive violence shall be prohibited. Scenes of brutal torture, excessive and unnecessary knife and gunplay, physical agony, the gory and gruesome crime shall be eliminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphic, gratuitous, or gory portrayals of violence were banned; publishers had to remove or tone down such scenes to obtain the CCA seal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminals must not be glamorized
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminals shall not be presented so as to be rendered glamorous or to occupy a position which creates a desire for emulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters engaging in crime could not be portrayed as role models or paragons; antiheroes who invite emulation would violate this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for authority figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Policemen, judges, government officials, and respected institutions shall never be presented in such a way as to create disrespect for established authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrayals that undermine public respect for institutions or officials were disallowed; corrupt officials could be shown only under restrictive conditions in later revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban on scenes of horror, depravity and sexual sadism
rubrics_metrics.description: All scenes of horror, excessive bloodshed, gory or gruesome crimes, depravity, lust, sadism, masochism shall not be permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A broad prohibition against horror-genre imagery and sexualized violence; this was enforced strictly in the original Code and later partially relaxed for 'classic tradition' treatments.

rubrics_metrics.name: No 'horror' or 'terror' in titles
rubrics_metrics.description: No comic magazine shall use the words "horror" or "terror" in its title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An explicit title-restriction intended to limit sensational marketing; publishers sometimes worked around content restrictions without using these words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of lurid or gruesome illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: All lurid, unsavory, gruesome illustrations shall be eliminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Artwork judged lurid or gruesome would be rejected; editors were expected to alter illustrations (clothe characters, remove gore) to comply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evil only to illustrate moral issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion of stories dealing with evil shall be used or shall be published only where the intent is to illustrate a moral issue and in no case shall evil be presented alluringly, nor so as to injure the sensibilities of the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories with evil themes must have clear moral framing and not present evil attractively; this informed editing decisions and rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good must triumph over evil; criminals punished
rubrics_metrics.description: In every instance good shall triumph over evil and the criminal punished for his misdeeds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative outcomes were evaluated: stories needed moral closure demonstrating that wrongdoing is not rewarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crime must be depicted as sordid and unpleasant
rubrics_metrics.description: If crime is depicted it shall be as a sordid and unpleasant activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portrayals that made crime exciting or glamorous were prohibited; crime scenes should emphasize negative consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on depictions of walking dead and similar supernatural elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes dealing with, or instruments associated with walking dead, torture, vampires and vampirism, ghouls, cannibalism, and werewolfism are prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Originally many horror and supernatural tropes were categorically banned; later revisions permitted some (e.g., vampires) if handled in the 'classic tradition' of respected literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban on profanity, obscenity and vulgarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Profanity, obscenity, smut, vulgarity, or words or symbols which have acquired undesirable meanings are forbidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language and symbols considered indecent were subject to censorship; editors removed or changed offending text or symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic drawing of female characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Females shall be drawn realistically without exaggeration of any physical qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art depicting exaggerated sexual characteristics was disallowed; anecdotes in the article note editors removing cleavage and redrawing clothing to comply.

rubrics_metrics.name: No suggestive or salacious illustration or posture
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestive and salacious illustration or suggestive posture is unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poses or imagery deemed sexually suggestive were rejected under the Code; this clause was later removed in revisions (1971) altering what was permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on advertising nudity and offensive presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Nudity with meretricious purpose and salacious postures shall not be permitted in the advertising of any product; clothed figures shall never be presented in such a way as to be offensive or contrary to good taste or morals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertising and cover/inside art had to follow the same decency standards; sexualized ads were explicitly banned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total ban on nudity and undue exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Nudity in any form is prohibited, as is indecent or undue exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complete prohibition of nudity in comics and associated materials under the 1954 Code.

rubrics_metrics.name: No depiction or hinting of illicit sex relations or sexual abnormalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Illicit sex relations are neither to be hinted at nor portrayed. Rape scenes, as well as sexual abnormalities, are unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sexual conduct outside accepted norms—including sexual violence and 'abnormalities'—were disallowed and could trigger rejection by the CCA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on sex perversion or inference thereof
rubrics_metrics.description: Sex perversion or any inference to same is strictly forbidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Broad categorical ban used to exclude LGBTQ+ content and other non-heteronormative portrayals under contemporary definitions used by the Code administrators.

rubrics_metrics.name: No depiction or suggestion of seduction or rape
rubrics_metrics.description: Seduction and rape shall never be shown or suggested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly forbids narrative treatment or even implication of sexual coercion; later revisions allowed some suggestion but not portrayal in limited circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catch-all: elements contrary to spirit of code are violations
rubrics_metrics.description: All elements or techniques not specifically mentioned herein, but which are contrary to the spirit and intent of the code, and are considered violations of good taste or decency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A general clause allowing the CCA to reject material not explicitly listed if it violates overall standards of good taste; this enabled administrators broad discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission and seal authorization process
rubrics_metrics.description: Members submitted comics to the CCA, which screened them for adherence to its code, then authorized the use of their seal on the cover if the book was found to be in compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural requirement: publishers had to submit pre-publication for review to receive the CCA seal; in practice distributors often refused non-seal comics, enforcing compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1971 revision — limited sympathetic depiction of criminals allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: Revised to allow for, among other things, the sometimes "sympathetic depiction of criminal behavior... [and] corruption among public officials" ("as long as it is portrayed as exceptional and the culprit is punished").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1971 changes relaxed some restrictions: sympathetic portrayals could appear only when clearly exceptional and the wrongdoer faces consequences; reflected evolving storytelling norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1971 revision — limited allowance for classic supernatural works
rubrics_metrics.description: Vampires, ghouls and werewolves... when handled in the classic tradition such as Frankenstein, Dracula, and other high calibre literary works written by Edgar Allan Poe, Saki, Conan Doyle and other respected authors whose works are read in schools around the world (were permitted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowed certain supernatural elements if presented in a literary/classic context; publishers and creators sometimes worked around bans (e.g., Marvel's use of the term 'zuvembie').

rubrics_metrics.name: 1971 revision — depiction of narcotics/drug addiction allowed if condemned
rubrics_metrics.description: The CCA revised the Code to permit the depiction of "narcotics or drug addiction" if presented "as a vicious habit".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After public-health-backed stories (e.g., Spider-Man drug arc) and governmental input, the Code permitted drug depiction only when clearly portrayed as harmful; some publishers ran drug stories without CCA approval to force change.
